1149.title: The force of imagination
1149.hook: imagination can make us ill or well (Essays 1.21)
1149.howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne turn to his essay on the force of imagination for its frank self-report: he describes how pictures in his own mind stir pain or relief in his body, and how others use that power.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was different roads: sometimes pity softens a conqueror, sometimes courage. Your line was different roads.

A passenger on a plane starts scratching their head. Two minutes later, the passenger behind them is scratching too. Nothing has landed on that second head. Only a picture in a mind has changed. Or someone at dinner describes a dentist's drill in detail, and around the table, jaws clench. Montaigne noticed this in himself and gave it an essay, which opens on a Latin saying of the scholars: a strong imagination produces the event.
screen: `AN ITCH ON A PLANE.` → `THE ROW BEHIND STARTS TOO.` → `A PICTURE DID THAT.`

segments.voice: First, the confession. Montaigne says plainly that he's one of the people imagination works on hardest. The sight of someone else's pain gives him a pain of his own. A man who keeps coughing near him makes his own lungs and throat feel raw. It isn't a theory. It's a report on his body. Second, the pin. He tells of a woman who was sure she'd swallowed a pin with her bread, and cried out that she could feel it stuck in her throat. Someone sensible guessed it was her imagination, made her throw up, and slipped a bent pin into what came up. Seeing it, she felt her pain lift. Third, the doctors. Physicians work on a patient's imagination too, Montaigne notes, winning belief with promises of a cure, so that imagination can do part of the work. In this essay, imagination can make us ill, and it can help make us well. Fourth, his honesty about his stories. He admits he can't vouch for every tale he borrows, and leaves them on the conscience of whoever told them. What matters to him is that they're possible, and that they show something true about how people are made. It's a careful line, and it fits the subject: an author who knows his own mind can run ahead of the facts. In a plain week, the force of imagination is the email you've decided is angry before you open it. Montaigne's move is to notice: the mind is making a picture, and the body is believing it.

Then bring to mind something you've been dreading this week, and notice your shoulders, stomach or jaw, though nothing in the room has changed. 1150.title: The woman who carried an ox
1150.hook: custom makes anything seem natural, until you travel (Essays 1.23)
1150.carry: what feels like nature is often custom
1150.howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne take his essay on custom as an invitation to see one's own habits as habits, while noting that he also counsels caution about overturning accepted laws.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the force of imagination: a picture in the mind that the body believes. Your line was it imagines.

Shoes off at the door, or shoes on in the house. Dinner at six, or dinner at ten. The fork in the left hand, or switched to the right. A kiss on one cheek, or two, or a handshake. To someone, each of these is simply how things are done. Then a trip, or a new in-law, or a roommate from somewhere else, and the obvious thing turns out to be a choice. Montaigne wrote an essay about that moment, and he opens it with a woman carrying a calf.
screen: `SHOES OFF, OR SHOES ON.` → `OBVIOUS, TO SOMEONE.` → `A WOMAN CARRYING A CALF.`

segments.voice: First, the story. A village woman, Montaigne tells us, got used to petting and carrying a calf from the day it was born, and because she never stopped, she was still carrying it when it was a full-grown ox. Whoever first told that story, he says, understood the power of custom. It grows a little every day, until we're carrying something enormous without noticing the weight. Second, the schoolmistress. Custom, Montaigne writes, is a violent and sly teacher. She sets up her authority softly, bit by bit, then shows a tyrant's face, and we no longer dare raise our eyes to her. Third, the handkerchief. He tells of a gentleman who blew his nose with his fingers and defended it: why wrap something dirty in fine linen and carry it around in our pockets? Montaigne admits the argument has some sense to it. Only habit had kept him from seeing how strange the handkerchief is. We notice strangeness in other countries' customs, he says, and miss it in our own. He goes further: even the rules of conscience, which we say come from nature, are born of custom. Fourth, the brake. Montaigne doesn't tell anyone to tear up the town's laws. A wise person, he says, keeps their judgment free inside, and outwardly still follows the accepted ways. Questioning a custom and overthrowing it are different things. Day to day, just custom is the pause before calling someone else's way weird.

segments.voice: Look around the room, or around your day, for one thing you do without ever deciding to: the way you fold towels, which side of the bed, what counts as on time. 1151.title: A well-made head
1151.hook: better a well-made head than a well-filled one (Essays 1.26)
1151.howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne's essay on the education of children take its line about a well-made head as a case for teaching judgment over memorization.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was just custom: the woman who carried a calf until it was an ox. Your line was just custom.

A trivia night at a bar. One team has a member who knows every capital, every element, every year a war ended. They win. Later that week, the same person is asked to help a friend decide whether to take a job in another city, and has nothing to offer but more facts. A head can be very full and still not very useful. In a long essay on how to raise a child, Montaigne draws exactly this line, in one plain phrase.
screen: `A WINNING TRIVIA TEAM.` → `NO HELP WITH A REAL CHOICE.` → `FULL, BUT NOT USEFUL.`

segments.voice: First, the line. When choosing a tutor for a child, Montaigne says, look for one with a well-made head rather than a well-filled one. Both would be good, he allows, but character and understanding matter more than learning. Second, the funnel. Teachers, he complains, keep shouting into children's ears as if pouring into a funnel, and the child's only job is to repeat what was said. He wants the opposite: let the student taste things, choose, and tell them apart. Sometimes the tutor opens the way; sometimes he lets the student open it. And he puts it bluntly: knowing something by heart is not knowing it. Third, the bees. Bees go from flower to flower taking what they like, but the honey they make is all their own; it's no longer thyme or marjoram. A student should do the same with what they borrow from books: turn it into their own judgment. Fourth, the test. How do you know someone has learned? Not by what they can recite. By how they live. Montaigne has a homely picture for it: if food comes back up just as it went down, it was never digested. Learning that comes out word for word hasn't been taken in. Away from the classroom, a well-made head can belong to the friend who knows few capitals but asks the one question that helps you decide.

segments.voice: Pick one idea from these days on the path that you could recite but maybe couldn't explain: water, the runaway horse, custom, different roads. Put it in your own words, in your head, as if telling a twelve-year-old at the kitchen table, with no quoting. If it falls apart, that's useful too; try again, plainer.

1152.title: Who are the barbarians?
1152.hook: Montaigne asks whether the peoples of Brazil that Europeans call savage are more barbaric than Europe's own wars (Essays 1.31)
1152.howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often take Of Cannibals as practice in turning a judgment around: before calling another people barbarous, look hard at what your own side does.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was a well-made head: a mind that can judge, not one stuffed with facts. Your line was well made, not full.

A pair of trousers. That's where today's essay lands. To get there, Montaigne travels a long way without leaving home. He starts with a man in his household who had lived a long time on the coast of Brazil, and who told him about the people there. He moves through what Europeans of his day said about those people. And he ends up back in France, in the middle of its own wars, carrying one question the whole way: who are the barbarians?
screen: `A JOKE ABOUT TROUSERS.` → `A REPORT FROM BRAZIL.` → `BACK TO FRANCE.`

segments.voice: First, the turn. The essay is called Of Cannibals. From what he's been told, Montaigne says, he finds nothing barbarous or savage in these people, except that each of us calls barbarous whatever isn't our own custom. Here the idea of custom gets teeth. Second, the mirror. He doesn't pretend the people he heard about were gentle. He describes them killing enemies in war and eating them. There is more barbarity, he says, in eating a man alive than dead: in tearing apart by torture a body that can still feel, and roasting it bit by bit. He says he has seen this done, not among old enemies but among neighbors and fellow citizens, under cover of piety and religion. He was describing his own country, in his own time. Third, the visitors. Some of these men came to France, and Montaigne records what struck them. They found it strange that so many tall, bearded, armed men would obey a child instead of choosing one of their own to lead. And they'd noticed some people stuffed with every good thing while others, whom they called their halves, begged at their doors, thin with hunger. They wondered why the hungry put up with it. Fourth, the trousers. The essay ends with a shrug in the reader's voice: not bad at all, but so what? They don't wear breeches. Montaigne lets his reader sneer, and the sneer gives the reader away. One honest note: he never went to Brazil. It all came secondhand, and he tells us whose hands.

Find one habit of theirs that looks odd to you, then turn it around the way Montaigne does: which habit of yours would look odd from their side of the table? Hold both for a while, without deciding who wins.

1153.title: A room behind the shop
1153.hook: keep a room behind the shop, all your own, where true freedom lives (Essays 1.39)
1153.carry: love the front; keep a room behind it
1153.howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often take the back shop as a daily habit: a short, protected stretch of time, kept free even in a full life of family and work.

segments.voice: Yesterday's question was who are the barbarians: each of us calls barbarous whatever isn't our own custom. Your line was that same question.

A parked car in the driveway, engine off, with somebody still sitting in it. The groceries can wait three more minutes. So can the people inside. Or the shower with the fan running, or the long way home from the store: a few minutes nobody else can reach. Montaigne had a spot like that, and a name for it. He didn't take the name from a monastery or a mountain. He took it from a shop.
screen: `A PARKED CAR, ENGINE OFF.` → `THREE MORE MINUTES.` → `A NAME FROM A SHOP.`

segments.voice: First, the room. In his essay Of Solitude, Montaigne says we should set aside a back shop, all our own, entirely free, where we keep our true liberty and our main retreat. Picture a small shop: out front, the counter, the customers, the bell on the door. Behind a curtain, a back room where the shopkeeper sits down. There, he says, we hold our ordinary talk with ourselves, so privately that nothing from outside gets in. Second, the people out front. This isn't a plan to run away. Have a spouse, children, goods, and above all health, if we can, he says. Just don't be so tied to them that our happiness hangs on them. Love the front of the shop; don't live only there. Third, the trip you can't take. Leaving the crowd, he says, isn't enough on its own. We carry our worries and wants with us, even into the quietest place. Moving to the country doesn't empty the mind. The retreat has to happen inside, or it doesn't happen. Fourth, belonging to yourself. In the same essay he writes that the greatest thing in the world is knowing how to belong to yourself. Not to your job, not to your reputation, not even, all the way down, to the people you love most. Last week we met his tower. The tower was a building. The back shop is portable: ten minutes, a closed door, and nothing to produce.

1154.title: Laughing and weeping
1154.hook: Democritus laughed at the world, Heraclitus wept; Montaigne prefers laughter (Essays 1.50)
1154.howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often take this essay as permission to meet human folly, their own first, with a laugh rather than despair, keeping cruelty out of it.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the back shop: a room all your own, behind the counter. Your line was the back shop.

Two philosophers step out of their front doors and look at the same street. The same crowd, the same squabbles, the same people hurrying to things that won't matter by next year. One of them laughs. The other one cries. Montaigne didn't invent the story; he found it in older writers. What he adds is a vote. Asked to pick a face for looking at the human race, himself included, he picks one, and his reason isn't about comfort.
screen: `ONE STREET, TWO PHILOSOPHERS.` → `ONE LAUGHS, ONE CRIES.` → `MONTAIGNE VOTES.`

segments.voice: First, the two faces. In his essay Of Democritus and Heraclitus, Montaigne says Democritus found the human condition vain and ridiculous, and never went out in public without a mocking, laughing face. Heraclitus, feeling pity for that same condition, went about with a sad face and eyes full of tears. Same world, opposite weather. Second, the vote. Montaigne prefers the laugh. Not, he says, because laughing is more pleasant than weeping, but because it's more disdainful. It condemns us more. It seems to him that we can't be looked down on as much as we deserve. That's sharper than a cheerful shrug. His laugh has an edge, and he points it at all of us, himself first. Third, the reason underneath. He doesn't think there's as much misery in us as there is vanity, or as much malice as foolishness. We're not so much wicked as silly; not so much tragic as empty-headed. Tears take our follies seriously, as if they were grand. A laugh cuts them back to their real size. Fourth, the gentle version. Montaigne's laughter can bite. Today's practice keeps the part that helps: laughing at self-importance, starting with our own. The email rewritten six times. The grudge over a parking spot. The fear of looking foolish, which is itself a little foolish. Seen from a step back, a lot of it is comedy.

1155.title: We are patchwork
1155.hook: we are all patchwork, and each piece plays its own game (Essays 2.1)
1155.howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often take this essay as a reason to go slow in judging anyone, themselves included, by a single act.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was laughing and weeping: Montaigne chose the laugh, because our trouble is less malice than folly. Your line was laugh, don't weep.

Calm in the meeting, furious in the parking lot. Patient with a stranger's toddler, short with your own mother. Generous on Monday, petty by Thursday. So which one is the real you? Montaigne takes up that question in the essay that opens the second book of the Essays, and his answer is uncomfortable and oddly freeing. It's all of them. And none of them stays in charge for long.
screen: `CALM HERE, FURIOUS THERE.` → `WHICH ONE IS REAL?` → `ALL OF THEM.`

segments.voice: First, the puzzle. In Of the Inconstancy of Our Actions, Montaigne says that people who study human behavior find nothing harder than fitting our actions together into one steady picture. We contradict ourselves so often that it's easier to believe we're changeable than consistent. So, he says, it's unfair to judge a person by a single act. Second, the image. We are all patchwork, he writes, so shapeless and mixed in our making that each piece, each moment, plays its own game. Then the line that stings: there's as much difference between us and ourselves as between us and other people. Third, the confession. He doesn't exempt himself. He turns his soul one way and shows one face, he says, then turns it and shows another. He finds in himself bashful and bold, talkative and silent, truthful and lying, generous and stingy, depending on which side he looks from. Fourth, the week's patches. Imagination, which can make us ill or well. Custom, which makes anything seem normal. A head well made, not full. Who are the barbarians? The back shop. Laugh, don't weep. Montaigne never sews these into one system, and he doesn't try. Each essay is a patch. This one is a mercy, in two directions: toward the person who snapped at you, and toward the you who snapped back.
screen: `HARD TO BE CONSISTENT.` · `EACH PIECE PLAYS ITS OWN GAME.` · `BOLD AND BASHFUL, BOTH.` · `A WEEK OF PATCHES.` · then, large: `PATCHWORK.`

segments.voice: Bring back one recent moment when you were at your best, steady, kind and clear, and another when you were somebody else, rushed, sharp, small. Don't choose which one is real; set them side by side like two squares of cloth. Both are yours, so breathe with both of them there.
We are patchwork. Montaigne's picture of a person: made of pieces, each moment playing its own game, as different from ourselves as from others. Today's word.
